posts.text:
AI is burning Big Tech's free cash flow:

The combined CapEx of Amazon, $AMZN, Alphabet, $GOOGL, Meta, $META, and Microsoft, $MSFT, rose +$36.9 billion in Q3 2026, to a record $201.9 billion.

This figure has more than doubled over the last 12 months and is up +356% since Q1 2024.

Big Tech has now spent $1.6 trillion on CapEx over the last 3 years.

Meanwhile, the combined free cash flow of these companies fell -$33.1 billion last quarter, to -$26.4 billion, its lowest on record.

Free cash flow among these firms has dropped -$88.2 billion over the last year.

Only Microsoft reported positive free cash flow in Q3.

Looking ahead, these 4 companies plan to spend another $232 billion on CapEx in Q4, potentially lifting their combined CapEx to a record $740 billion in 2026.

Big Tech is undertaking one of the largest infrastructure buildouts in history.

posts.name: SMX 🇺🇸
posts.text:
Naval Ravikant once shared a story about Bill Gates shorting Tesla, a bet that could ultimately cost him more than $10 billion.

Gates had taken a massive short position against Tesla, reportedly equivalent to roughly 1% of the company’s total shares.

Naval suggested that if Tesla became the world’s most valuable company by a wide margin, the losses could be so enormous that even someone as wealthy as Bill Gates could face financial ruin.

But what fascinated Naval wasn't the money. It was Elon Musk’s reaction.

Musk was genuinely confused. How could someone who publicly championed clean energy financially bet against a company working to accelerate the world's transition to sustainable energy?

To Gates, it was reportedly just a financial decision. But to Musk, it was something much deeper.

According to Naval, that moment revealed something fundamental about Elon Musk.

posts.text:
Hey @grok 

Explain how the one-day Friday selloff in the tech sector ranked historically in tech selloffs in one-day moves based on total tech market cap loss and total capital lost by investors.

posts.name: Steve Burns
posts.text:
One of the most useful things to measure after earnings isn't the size of the gap.

Measure how much of that gap survives.
A stock that gaps 12% and keeps 11% has processed the new information very differently from one that gaps 12% and finishes up 2%.

The announcement creates the gap.
The price action afterward tells you what traders ultimately decided about the move.
